title: How Cannibalism Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss cannibalism, opening with the recent Greyhound bus killing in Manitoba allegedly committed by Vince Lee, then the case of Armin Meiwes, who advertised for a victim and ate a consenting man, Jurgen Brandes, in Germany and was tried for manslaughter and then murder because Germany had no law against cannibalism. They discuss the lack of cannibalism statutes in the US and UK, pathological cannibalism (Albert Fish, Jeffrey Dahmer), and anthropological categories: survival, learned/customary, endocannibalism, exocannibalism, and autocannibalism. Examples include the Donner Party, the Andes rugby crash (Alive), the custom of the sea lot-drawing practice, Beth Conklin's work with the Wari' in the Amazon, the Fore of Papua New Guinea, the 1930s lynching of Claude Neal in Florida, and forced autocannibalism in the Congo. They close with materialist versus idealist theories of why cultures practice cannibalism, and the hosts joke about eating each other and go get food.

segments.title: Opening banter and Greyhound bus murder
segments.summary: Hosts open with a discussion of the alleged Greyhound bus killing in Manitoba by Vince Lee, including the stabbing, beheading and cannibalism, and explain why it was passed over as a lead for their cannibalism article.

segments.title: Armin Meiwes and consensual cannibalism
segments.summary: Armin Meiwes advertised for a man willing to be eaten and killed Jurgen Brandes, who had come to him, after they ate his penis. Meiwes butchered and ate about four pounds of his body over months; he was caught after chat room users alerted police.

segments.title: Legal status of cannibalism
segments.summary: Germany had no law against cannibalism, so Meiwes was tried first for manslaughter and then retried for murder amid public outrage. The hosts say they found no US federal statute against cannibalism and no UK law, and that taboo functions beyond the law.

segments.title: Pathological cannibalism
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish pathological cannibalism, illustrated by Meiwes, Vince Lee, Albert Fish and Jeffrey Dahmer, from the anthropological study of cannibalism.

segments.title: Types of cannibalism and autocannibalism
segments.summary: They list categories: survival, learned, endocannibalism (within the group), exocannibalism (outside the group), pathological, and autocannibalism. They discuss biting nails as a mild form of autocannibalism and forced autocannibalism cases in the Congo.

segments.title: Claude Neal lynching in Florida
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1930s Florida lynching of Claude Neal by about two thousand white Southerners, in which he was tortured, forced to eat his penis and to say he liked it, and then hanged; they note such events are not taught in history classes.

segments.title: Survival cannibalism and custom of the sea
segments.summary: They cover survival cannibalism, citing the Donner Party and the Andes crash depicted in Alive, and the nineteenth-century custom of the sea, in which lots were drawn to select who would be killed and eaten.

segments.title: Learned cannibalism and funeral rites
segments.summary: Learned or customary cannibalism is discussed, including endocannibalism as a funeral rite among the Fore of Papua New Guinea and the Wari' of the Amazon, where anthropologist Beth Conklin studied grief practices, and the Fore's practice of gaining attributes by eating certain body parts.

segments.title: Materialism vs idealism theories
segments.summary: The hosts outline the materialist view, that cannibalism arises from necessity, versus the idealist view, that it arises from symbolic thinking. Josh leans toward materialism.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts joke about eating each other, mention the show's feedback address, and end the episode by deciding to get food.
